content: Enteroviruses are a group of positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses that are known to cause a variety of diseases in humans and other mammals. Through serologic studies, 66 distinct human enterovirus serotypes have been identified based on antibody neutralization tests. Furthermore, within several of these serotypes, additional antigenic variants have been recognized due to reduced or nonreciprocal cross-neutralization between different strains. Initially, enteroviruses were classified into four groups based on their pathogenesis in humans and animals: polioviruses, Coxsackie A viruses (CA), Coxsackie B viruses (CB), and echoviruses. However, it was soon discovered that there were significant overlaps in the biological characteristics of viruses within these groups. More recently, newly identified enteroviruses have been named sequentially, such as EV68, EV69, EV70, and EV71. Enteroviruses are present in respiratory secretions, such as saliva, sputum, or nasal mucus, as well as in the stool of infected individuals. Transmission occurs through direct contact with these secretions or stool, or via contact with contaminated surfaces or objects, such as drinking glasses or telephones. Individuals who care for young children, such as parents, teachers, and childcare workers, are at particular risk of infection, especially during diaper changes when hands may become contaminated with stool from an infected infant or toddler. Non-polio enterovirus infections are caused by enteroviruses, which are composed of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and protein. This group includes polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and other enteroviruses. Beyond the three types of polioviruses, there are over 60 types of non-polio enteroviruses that can cause disease in humans. These viruses are highly prevalent and are second only to rhinoviruses (the viruses responsible for the common cold) as the most frequent viral infectious agents in humans. Non-polio enteroviruses are responsible for an estimated 10 to 15 million or more symptomatic infections annually in the United States. Thanks to widespread vaccination efforts, all three types of polioviruses have been eradicated from the Western Hemisphere, as well as the Western Pacific and European regions. However, non-polio enteroviruses remain a significant cause of illness. Individuals who frequently come into contact with young children, such as parents, teachers, and childcare workers, are at increased risk of infection due to potential hand contamination during diaper changes. While anyone can become infected with non-polio enteroviruses, certain factors, such as age and seasonal variations, can increase the likelihood of infection. Most individuals infected with non-polio enteroviruses remain asymptomatic. For those who do develop symptoms, the clinical presentation is typically mild and may include upper respiratory symptoms resembling a summer cold, a flu-like illness characterized by fever and muscle aches, or a rash-associated illness.
